newsitem.title: USA: Food Lion argues for damages in US suit.
newsitem.headline: Food Lion argues for damages in US suit.

text.p: Lawyers for grocery chain Food Lion Inc. told a federal judge on Saturday that the grocer sought $1.7 billion in damages from ABC television in order to recoup losses from an expose the network aired.

Food Lion, the U.S. unit of Belgian retailer Ets Delhaize Freres et Cie "LE LION' SA, claims it lost $1.5 billion in stock value at the time of the Nov. 5, 1992 broadcast, and $233 million in profits after the broadcast.
U.S. District Judge N. Carlton Tilley did not make a decision in the rare Saturday session and was not expected to do so until much later in the trial.

Food Lion, based in Salisbury, North Carolina, is suing ABC and four of its producers, charging the network committed civil fraud, trespassing and other criminal offenses during an undercover investigation for a "PrimeTime Live" show.
ABC, based in New York, is a unit of Walt Disney Co.
The show claimed the company used unsanitary food practices and sold spoiled meat.
Tilley already ruled Food Lion cannot collect damages stemming from the broadcast unless the grocer can prove that the story was false and ABC knew it.
But while Food Lion maintains the story was false, it was not making that the basis of its lawsuit.

Food Lion lawyers told the judge on Saturday the grocer should still be allowed to ask for losses in sales and stock value because ABC would not have had a story to broadcast if not for the allegedly fraudulent hidden-camera investigation.
"Without this tape, the show would not have aired," Wyatt said. "I don't see what Food Lion is doing as an unprincipled attack on the news media's right to gather information."
ABC attorney Nathan Siegel said Food Lion's losses stem not from the network's methods but from the revelation of true, embarrassing information.

"It is not the existence of a broadcast that harmed Food Lion," Siegel said. "It was the content of the broadcast that harmed Food Lion. It is caused by its truth. It is caused by what Food Lion did."

In trial testimony on Friday, an ABC producer working undercover at a Myrtle Beach, South Carolina store said a Food Lion superviser told her to sell 3-weeks-old macaroni salad. But earlier in the week, the producer said she lied on an application to get a job at that store -- an act that the grocery company calls fraud.
The judge was not expected to rule on the damages question until later in the trial when he'll have to instruct the jury on how to make an award provided ABC is found liable.
